🔔 Can DATA Network bring lasting activity to Sui? 

📣 DATA Network plans to retire its independent chain and run its AI training data registry on Sui, with Walrus handling files. Sui Foundation is investing $30 million in the network. A registry that its backers say already records millions of receipts daily could bring activity to Sui; how much of that translates into recurring SUI demand remains an open question.

⭐️ Sui Foundation’s October 12 announcement  says Trace, a rights registry for AI training data, is joining its stack. Walrus will store encrypted original files and Sui will record programmable rights and settlements. DATA Network’s own chain will eventually close. The foundation says its $30 million commitment makes it the largest institutional holder of the DATA Network, alongside PIP Labs and the DATA Foundation. The statement does not publish a completed migration date or a dollar amount of fees the business expects to pay on Sui. 

⚠️ Trace registers a data contribution, its origin and the rights attached to it. The foundation says the system has processed more than 250 million contributions since a June launch and averages over 3 million receipts a day. Applications named in the announcement include Kled, Numo and Oto. Kled is described as an opt in human data marketplace with more than 1.5 billion records being onboarded. Those are participant supplied operational claims; the release does not contain an independently audited breakdown by customer, chain, fee or paying AI lab. 

🔖 DATA Foundation says Trace settles payments to contributors when their data is licensed. A nurse’s consented account, a dashcam clip or a factory worker’s demonstration might be recorded as training material with use rights. The registry entry is not necessarily the complete source file. Its design separates a claim about who supplied data and who may use it from storage of the bytes. Sui and Walrus are meant to handle those parts after migration.

Following up on the previous post about US Treasuries.

It’s quite symbolic that The Economist recently featured a cover asking “Will Bonds Blow Up?” and warning of an impending sovereign debt crisis.

There are growing concerns that it’s becoming increasingly expensive for the US to borrow money. Investors are demanding higher and higher yields amid massive debt, budget deficits, and inflation risks. But there’s an interesting paradox here. While we’re focused on the US, the debt problem could blow up much sooner somewhere else entirely.

Take France, for example. It’s the second-largest economy in the European Union. Its public debt is approaching 120% of GDP this year, the budget deficit is around 5.4%, and 10-year bond yields have nearly reached 5%, their highest levels since 2002. For comparison, when Greece’s sovereign debt crisis began in 2009, its debt stood at around 127% of GDP. To be fair, its budget deficit was much worse, exceeding 15%. So France today is certainly not Greece in 2009, but some of the numbers are starting to look uncomfortably familiar.

And this is where things get really interesting. If France’s problems turn into a full-blown debt crisis, we’re no longer talking about a small country on the periphery of Europe. France accounts for nearly 16% of the EU’s entire economy. A crisis of that scale would almost certainly push investors to look for the safest and most liquid places to park their capital.

Some money is already flowing out of French bonds and into German bonds, the Swiss franc, and the US dollar. If the situation becomes truly systemic, US Treasuries could once again become an obvious destination. Demand for them would rise, bond prices would go up, yields would fall, and suddenly it would become cheaper for America to borrow.

And that’s the key takeaway. There are no perfect assets and no perfect countries in the markets. Capital always goes where it sees the best available alternative. That’s why a scenario in which Europe experiences a debt crisis before the US could actually turn the dollar and US Treasuries into beneficiaries of the very crisis that everyone in America is so worried about right now. For investors, that’s yet another reason not to bet everything on a single scenario and to keep a close eye not just on the US, but also on what’s happening with European debt.

An Ethereum Foundation researcher suggests pre-transferring large sums to addresses that have not yet signed any transactions

On October 7th, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake called on the crypto industry to calmly prepare for a scenario in which the ECDSA signature scheme could be hacked before the advent of a quantum computer. In his estimation, in the worst case, this could be a matter of months, not years. There is no confirmed method for such a hack.

Drake described the hack as rapid recovery of a private key from an already disclosed public one: for example, in about a week with available hardware such as a large cluster of graphics processors. According to him, it is now reasonable to prepare for such a possibility. He linked the warning to recent progress in mathematical models, including the publication of a set of mathematical works by OpenAI's internal model. The main risk, according to Drake, concerns addresses that have already signed transactions and thus revealed their public key. He recommends that large and prepared holders transfer most of their funds to addresses that have not signed anything yet. After each outgoing transaction, it is also better to transfer the remainder to a new address. You don't need a new wallet for this: you can get the address from the same seed phrase.

Drake specifically asks not to rush. According to him, there is cause for action, but a hasty transfer can do more harm than good. For wallets with less than 50 bitcoins, he sees partial coverage in already disclosed Satoshi addresses: around 20 thousand addresses with 50 bitcoins each. For oracle operators and second-layer network security advisors, he recommends changing the ECDSA key after each signed message or supplementing the signature with a hash-based scheme, such as SPHINCS.

According to his estimation, one can only exit this regime with cryptography designed for the period after the current development of artificial intelligence. Drake himself leans towards hash-based schemes and moving away from cryptography that relies on elliptic curves, lattices, or isogenies. In November, he plans to discuss the topic with institutional participants at a meeting in London.
